planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Cabernet Sauvignon is a late-ripening variety needing a long, warm season, and its thick skin gives it useful resistance to rot in humid climates compared with thinner-skinned varieties.

directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Cabernet Sauvignon is the world's most widely planted premium red wine grape, a natural cross of Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc first identified in 17th-century Bordeaux, prized for small, thick-skinned, deeply pigmented berries that yield full-bodied, tannic red wines with characteristic blackcurrant and cassis notes and strong aging potential. The thick skin that defines the variety also gives it better resistance to fruit rot than many thinner-skinned grapes, a real advantage in humid climates, though the late ripening window still means the vine needs a long, warm growing season to fully mature fruit before fall. Train young vines to a permanent trellis, manage the canopy for good sun exposure and air movement around developing clusters, and harvest based on sugar and acid balance rather than a fixed date, since ripening timing varies by site and season.
sources: University of California Davis Viticulture and Enology

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Merlot ripens earlier than Cabernet Sauvignon and its thinner skin makes it somewhat more prone to rot in wet or humid conditions.

directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Merlot is one of the great Bordeaux red wine grapes, historically blended with Cabernet Sauvignon but equally prized as a varietal wine in its own right, producing softer, rounder, fruit-forward wines with plum and blackberry notes and generally gentler tannins than Cabernet Sauvignon. The vine buds and ripens earlier than Cabernet Sauvignon, which can be an advantage in shorter growing seasons but also increases the risk of spring frost damage to young growth and demands closer attention to disease management, since the thinner-skinned berries are more susceptible to bunch rot in wet or humid weather. Train to a permanent trellis, manage the canopy for airflow around clusters, and monitor closely as harvest approaches, since Merlot can lose acidity quickly once sugar accumulation begins in earnest.
sources: University of California Davis Viticulture and Enology

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Gewürztraminer is a cool-climate variety that performs best where warm days are balanced by cool nights, and it struggles with vigor and disease pressure in hot, humid regions.

directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Gewürztraminer, a pink-to-russet-skinned variety most closely associated with Alsace, France and Germany, is grown for intensely aromatic wines carrying strong floral, lychee, rose, and warm spice notes unlike almost any other white grape, a character so distinctive that the German word 'gewürz,' meaning spiced, was appended to the older Traminer name to describe it. The vine is only moderately vigorous and can be somewhat inconsistent in fruit set, and it performs best in cooler climates with a wide gap between warm days and cool nights, which helps preserve the delicate aromatics that define good Gewürztraminer wine. Train to a permanent trellis, thin crop if fruit set is heavy to concentrate flavor, and harvest based on aromatic development as much as sugar level, since the variety's signature perfume can be lost if fruit hangs too long in hot conditions.
sources: University of California Davis Viticulture and Enology

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Chenin Blanc is a vigorous, adaptable variety that tolerates a wider range of climates than many fine wine grapes, including reasonably warm regions.

directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Chenin Blanc originated in the Loire Valley of France and stands out among fine wine grapes for its remarkable versatility, capable of producing bone-dry still wines, off-dry and sweet dessert wines, and high-quality sparkling wines all from the same naturally high-acid, honey-and-quince-flavored fruit, depending on when it is picked and how it is vinified. The vigorous, productive vine is more heat-tolerant and adaptable than many classic white wine varieties, giving it a genuine practical advantage in warmer growing regions where more delicate cool-climate grapes struggle to retain acidity. Train to a permanent trellis, manage vigor through canopy work and crop thinning since the variety can overproduce if left unchecked, and choose harvest timing deliberately based on the intended wine style, since Chenin Blanc's high natural acidity gives growers real flexibility in when to pick.
sources: University of California Davis Viticulture and Enology
